spans.assertion: the analysis used data from 1,419 professional players across four European leagues, 2012-2013 season
the primary estimand (adjusted risk difference) was found to be 0.062 percentage points (95% CI -0.009% to 0.134%, p=0.072), not statistically significant
the secondary estimand (adjusted odds ratio) was found to be 0.910 (95% CI 0.697-1.189, p=0.490), also non-significant
several rate-based models suggested a ~15% higher red-card rate for dark-skinned players (rate ratio ≈1.15)
these rate-based estimates become non-significant when properly accounting for clustering and when using the primary estimand
a sensitivity analysis using continuous skin tone found a statistically significant dose-response relationship (p=0.007) that conflicts with the primary binary analysis
overall conclusion is that the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED because of inconsistency across modeling approaches, the borderline primary p-value, and a wide CI including zero
the risk difference was defined as the percentage-point change in red-card probability comparing dark skin (≥0.5) to light skin (<0.5), adjusted for position, league, height, and weight
used Poisson regression with a log(games) offset at player level, followed by marginal standardization
confidence intervals and p-values were obtained via non-parametric bootstrap with 2,000 iterations
point estimate of the risk difference was 0.0618 percentage points
two-sided p-value was 0.072
dark-skinned players are estimated to receive 0.062 additional red cards per 100 games versus light-skinned players, adjusting for confounders
the 95% CI includes zero, so the difference is not statistically significant at α=0.05
the bootstrap distribution was approximately normal, verified by a Q-Q plot, supporting validity of the percentile-based CI
the odds ratio was defined as the odds of ever receiving a red card, dark vs light skin, adjusted for the same covariates
used logistic regression at player level
point estimate odds ratio was 0.910
two-sided p-value was 0.490
dark-skinned players have 9% lower odds of ever receiving a red card, but this is highly uncertain and not statistically significant
the CI includes 1.0, i.e. no effect
this odds-ratio result contradicts the rate-based Poisson models, suggesting any effect may lie in frequency of cards among those who receive them rather than in who receives them
unit of analysis was player, N=1,419
total player-referee dyads in the dataset: 146,028
dyads with skin-tone ratings: 124,621 (85.3%)
players included in the primary analysis: 1,419 (89.5% of those with photos)
unique referees: 2,978
total games: 350,448
total red cards: 1,478
overall red-card rate: 4.22 per 1,000 games
dark skin was defined as skin tone ≥0.5 on the 0-1 scale (n=330, 23.3%)
light skin was defined as skin tone <0.5 (n=1,089, 76.7%)
skin tone was measured by averaging two independent rater scores (5-point scale rescaled 0-1)
inter-rater correlation was r=0.92
adjusted for position category, league country, height, and weight as covariates
position is a strong confounder: defenders receive red cards at 5.50 per 1,000 games vs 3.51 for forwards
dark-skinned players have different position distributions (e.g. only 4% goalkeepers vs 13% for light-skinned) and league distributions (34% in France vs 13% for light-skinned)
height and weight were included to control for physicality
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) for missing skin tone (no photo)
excluded 152 players (9.6% of those with photos) for missing position
excluded 24 players for missing height/weight
total excluded from the adjusted analysis: 166 players (10.5%)
players without photos had substantially more missing position data (43% unknown) and different red-card rates, suggesting non-random missingness
among players with complete data, there was no evidence that missingness differed systematically by skin tone conditional on covariates
skin tone was created by averaging rater1 and rater2, then dichotomized at 0.5 (the theoretical midpoint)
games were log-transformed and used as an offset in the Poisson models
no other transformations were applied to the outcome or covariates
primary estimand used bootstrap SE with 2,000 iterations (resampling players with replacement)
secondary estimand used maximum-likelihood SEs from logistic regression
sensitivity analyses used cluster-robust SEs clustered by player for dyad-level models
significance level was set at α=0.05, two-sided tests
no multiple-testing correction was applied, on the grounds of a single primary hypothesis
the primary analysis used 0.5 as the skin-tone dichotomization cutoff; alternative thresholds were also tested
at threshold 0.25 (median): rate ratio 1.141 (95% CI 1.023-1.272, p=0.017)
at threshold 0.375 (upper tertile): rate ratio 1.149 (95% CI 1.024-1.289, p=0.018)
at threshold 0.50 (midpoint, primary): rate ratio 1.150 (95% CI 1.014-1.304, p=0.030)
rate ratios are consistent (~1.14-1.15) across thresholds, but statistical significance varies, with lower thresholds yielding stronger significance
skin tone was used as a continuous predictor (0-1 scale) in a sensitivity analysis
rate ratio per 1-unit increase in skin tone: 1.292 (95% CI 1.074-1.553, p=0.007)
rate ratio per 0.5-unit increase (light to dark): 1.136 (95% CI 1.036-1.246)
this suggests a significant dose-response relationship, with darker skin associated with a higher red-card rate
this dose-response result conflicts with the primary binary analysis and may reflect overfitting or non-linear relationships
analyzed at the dyad level (n=115,603) with cluster-robust SEs by player, instead of aggregating to player level
dyad-level rate ratio: 1.150 (95% CI 0.989-1.337, p=0.070)
the point estimate is identical to the player-level model, but accounting for within-player clustering increases the SE, rendering the effect non-significant
this dyad-level result is consistent with the primary analysis bootstrap result
ran an analysis without adjustment for covariates
unadjusted rate ratio: 1.142 (95% CI 1.014-1.285, p=0.028)
the crude association is significant, but the adjusted estimate is nearly identical, suggesting confounding is minimal
14.7% of dyads were missing skin tone due to unavailable photos
players without photos differ systematically, having more missing position data and possibly being lower-tier players
complete-case analysis assumes the data are missing at random (text is corrupted/truncated at this point in the source)
raters assessed skin tone from static photos, which may not reflect how referees perceive players in real time (lighting, distance, motion)
high inter-rater reliability (r=0.92) suggests measurement error is modest, though systematic bias in photo-based ratings cannot be ruled out
dichotomization at the arbitrary 0.5 threshold may misclassify players and reduce power
sensitivity analyses showed robustness to threshold choice, but continuous models gave different results
adjusted for position, league, and anthropometrics, but did not adjust for playing style, team quality, player behavior/reputation, or referee characteristics beyond country-level implicit bias
a supplementary analysis tested interaction with referee implicit bias (IAT scores) and found no significant moderation (p=0.535), at the country level
used games played as the exposure measure, an imperfect proxy since it does not capture minutes played
minutes played would have been the preferable exposure measure but were not available
red cards are rare events (4.22 per 1,000 games), limiting power to detect small effects despite the large sample
the 95% CI for the risk difference spans a 14-fold range (-0.009% to 0.134%), precluding strong conclusions
a single primary hypothesis was pre-specified

multiple sensitivity analyses with different modeling choices were conducted, and without pre-registration it cannot be definitively resolved whether inconsistent results reflect false positives or true effects obscured by methodology

spans.note: caveat that results may not generalize beyond the 2012-2013 season and these four leagues

spans.assertion: the skin-tone distribution is right-skewed (76.7% light skin), limiting power to detect effects in the smaller dark-skinned subgroup
defenders receive red cards at 2.6x the rate of midfielders (5.50 vs 3.44 per 1,000 games)
dark-skinned players are underrepresented as goalkeepers (4.2% vs 13.4%) and overrepresented as forwards (18.9% vs 11.6%)
adjustment for position reduced the rate ratio only slightly (1.142→1.150), indicating the crude association is not primarily driven by position
France has the highest red-card rate (rate ratio vs England 1.41, p<0.001)
dark-skinned players are concentrated in France (34% vs 13% for light-skinned), though adjustment did not materially change estimates
referee country-level implicit bias (IAT) scores predict overall red-card rates (β=3.29, p=0.013)
there was no significant interaction between player skin tone and referee implicit bias (β=-1.21, p=0.535), contrary to the hypothesis that bias would amplify effects for dark-skinned players
primary finding: adjusted risk difference of 0.062 percentage points (95% CI -0.009% to 0.134%, p=0.072), not statistically significant
secondary finding: adjusted odds ratio of 0.910 (95% CI 0.697-1.189, p=0.490), non-significant and in the opposite direction from the hypothesis
overall assessment is that the hypothesis is NOT SUPPORTED, since the ~15% higher rate suggested by rate-based models becomes non-significant under proper analysis
non-significance holds when properly accounting for clustering (p=0.070), using the pre-specified primary estimand (p=0.072), and examining the binary outcome (p=0.490)
the evidence is inconclusive; the primary CI spans a small protective effect to a modest harmful effect, and the p=0.072 point estimate is only marginally non-significant
the continuous skin-tone model showed a significant dose-response (p=0.007), but this conflicts with the binary analysis and may reflect Type I error from multiple modeling approaches
even at the CI upper bound (0.134%), the effect translates to about 1.3 additional red cards per 1,000 games, or ~0.4 over a typical ~300-game career — a small, debatable effect

given the uncertainty, borderline p-values, conflicting results, and potential unmeasured confounding, they conclude they cannot determine that referees differentially issue red cards based on skin tone
they recommend future research with more granular exposure data (minutes played), better measurement of playing style and referee-player history, larger samples, and pre-registered analysis plans
such future research would be needed to definitively test the hypothesis; the current data, while suggestive, do not provide convincing evidence
all analyses are fully reproducible from the provided Python script, which generates all reported estimates/CIs/p-values, the sensitivity analyses, and diagnostic plots
used random seed 42 for bootstrap replicability
unadjusted player-level rate ratio was 1.142 (95% CI 1.014-1.285, p=0.028), significant
adjusted player-level rate ratio was 1.150 (95% CI 1.014-1.304, p=0.030), significant
primary risk difference was 0.0618 percentage points (95% CI -0.0092-0.1339, p=0.072), not significant
secondary odds ratio was 0.910 (95% CI 0.697-1.189, p=0.490), not significant
dyad-level cluster-robust rate ratio was 1.150 (95% CI 0.989-1.337, p=0.070), not significant
continuous skin-tone rate ratio per 0.5 unit was 1.136 (95% CI 1.036-1.246, p=0.007), significant

sample characteristics differ modestly by skin-tone group — e.g. light-skin N=1,089 (76.7%) vs dark-skin N=330 (23.3%), similar mean height/weight/games, but differing position distribution and red-card rate (4.07 vs 4.68 per 1,000 games)
conclusion restated: hypothesis NOT SUPPORTED, insufficient evidence that referees differentially issue red cards to dark- vs light-skinned players
